name: Frederick the Great
info: Frederick II, King in Prussia and later King of Prussia from 1740 to 1786, who seized Silesia, held it through the Seven Years' War, took part in the First Partition of Poland and patronised the Enlightenment.

facts.born: 24 January 1712, in the Berlin Palace; son of Crown Prince Frederick William of Prussia and Sophia Dorothea of Hanover, of the House of Hohenzollern
facts.died: 17 August 1786, in an armchair in his study at Sanssouci, Potsdam, aged 74; childless
facts.role: Crown prince from 1713; King in Prussia from 1740; King of Prussia from 1772 until his death in 1786
facts.known: the conquest of Silesia; the Seven Years' War; the First Partition of Poland; enlightened absolutism and the ruler as 'first servant of the state'; reform of the army, courts and civil service; flute music and patronage of the arts; Sanssouci

t: Frederick took Silesia from Austria in the 1740s and kept it through the Seven Years' War against a coalition of Austria, France, Russia, Sweden and the Holy Roman Empire, at a heavy cost in lives and money.

He called the sovereign the first servant of the state, reformed the courts and civil service, curbed judicial torture and invited settlers of any faith, while keeping Protestantism favoured and Jews and Catholics under limits.

In 1772 he annexed most of Royal Prussia in the First Partition of Poland and set out to Germanise its people, a side of his rule that sits beside his reputation as a patron of music, letters and science.
dyk: Frederick composed 121 sonatas for flute and continuo, and visitors to his grave at Sanssouci often leave potatoes on the stone in honour of his promotion of the crop in Prussia.
ev: Frederick's attempt to flee to Britain fails, and he is forced to watch the beheading of his friend Hans Hermann von Katte at Küstrin
Frederick becomes king and invades Silesia, beginning the First Silesian War
The Treaty of Dresden confirms Prussia's hold on Silesia, and Frederick is first called 'the Great'
Frederick invades Saxony, starting the Third Silesian War and the wider Seven Years' War
Austrian and Russian forces rout Frederick's army at the Battle of Kunersdorf
The Treaty of Hubertusburg ends the war, and Prussia keeps Silesia
Frederick annexes most of Royal Prussia in the First Partition of Poland and takes the title King of Prussia
Frederick dies at Sanssouci and is succeeded by his nephew Frederick William II

sections.early:
Frederick was born in the Berlin Palace on 24 January 1712, the son of the then Crown Prince Frederick William of Prussia and Sophia Dorothea of Hanover. His grandfather Frederick I welcomed the birth, as two earlier grandsons had died in infancy. When Frederick I died in 1713, his son became King Frederick William I, the 'Soldier King', and the boy became crown prince. Frederick had nine siblings who lived to adulthood, among them his eldest sister Wilhelmine, with whom he stayed close until her death in 1758.

Frederick William I had a violent temper, ruled with absolute authority and built a large army, while Sophia Dorothea, daughter of the future George I of Britain, was learned and polite; the differences between the parents shaped the son. Frederick was taught French and German, many of his tutors were French Calvinists, and his later teachers in languages, classics, history and rhetoric were Jacques Duhan de Jandun and Maturin Veyssière La Croze. The king wanted an education that was religious and practical and ordered that his heir not be taught predestination.

The young Frederick preferred music, literature and French culture. His father thought these interests effeminate and often beat and humiliated him. With Duhan's help, Frederick built a secret library of 3,000 volumes of poetry, Greek and Roman classics and philosophy.
sections.rise:
At 16 Frederick grew attached to the king's page Peter Karl Christoph von Keith, who was sent away when the king heard rumours. Frederick was almost certainly homosexual, though the extent of their intimacy remains ambiguous. After plans to marry him to a British princess collapsed, he planned to flee to Britain with Hans Hermann von Katte and other young officers. The plot was betrayed in August 1730; both were arrested and accused of treason, and the king made Frederick watch Katte's beheading at Küstrin on 6 November. Frederick was pardoned that month but kept at Küstrin to study administration.

His release in 1732 came on condition that he marry Elisabeth Christine of Brunswick-Bevern, a Protestant relative of the Habsburgs. He wrote that there could be 'neither love nor friendship between us', but married her on 12 June 1733; they had no children and lived apart once he was king. Restored to the army in 1732, he served under Prince Eugene of Savoy in the War of the Polish Succession and noted the weakness of the imperial army.

At Schloss Rheinsberg he gathered musicians and actors and wrote the Anti-Machiavel, published anonymously in 1740. That year his father died, the two reconciled at the end, and Frederick, aged 28, inherited a heavily militarised state whose army was the fourth largest in Europe.
sections.deeds:
Frederick declined to endorse the Pragmatic Sanction and, after Emperor Charles VI died in October 1740, invaded Silesia on 16 December on the basis of old and ambiguous Hohenzollern claims. The province nearly doubled Prussia's population and added a third to its territory. Victories at Mollwitz in 1741, where he fled the field and later called the battle his school, and at Chotusitz in 1742 won it by the Treaty of Breslau; in the Second Silesian War he won at Hohenfriedberg and Soor, and the Treaty of Dresden of 25 December 1745 confirmed his gains.

In 1756 he invaded neutral Saxony and began the Seven Years' War. He won at Prague, Rossbach and Leuthen but lost at Kolín, Hochkirch and Kunersdorf, where almost half his army was destroyed. Prussia was saved when Empress Elizabeth of Russia died in January 1762 and Peter III made peace; the Treaty of Hubertusburg of 1763 left Silesia with Prussia.

At home he protected industry with tariffs, extended press freedom, abolished most judicial torture and, with Samuel von Cocceji, reformed the courts, work that led to the Prussian Law Code of 1794. He drained the Oderbruch marshes, founded about 1,200 villages and promoted the potato. He reinstituted the Berlin Academy, recruited Euler and Lagrange, built the Berlin State Opera and Sanssouci, and composed flute music.
sections.opponents:
His invasion of neutral Saxony in 1756 and his forcible enlistment of the captured Saxon army brought him widespread international criticism. To pay for the war he debased the Prussian coin five times, and the coinage of Saxony and Poland, which covered over 20 per cent of its cost but caused massive inflation; Saxony was left nearly destitute. The war badly depleted Prussia's population and army and killed the best of its officers.

Poland suffered most from his policy. He had compared it to an 'artichoke, ready to be consumed leaf by leaf', opposed Polish reform, inflated its currency with Polish coin dies for profits above 25 million thalers, and bombarded Polish customs ports on the Vistula. After the partition he called the inhabitants of Polish Prussia 'slovenly Polish trash' and aimed to remove the Poles through Germanisation: crown lands and monasteries seized, a military draft, German settlement and taxes that impoverished the Polish nobility.

His tolerance had limits. Catholics were kept out of higher office, Church property in Polish Prussia was confiscated, and in his Testament politique he wrote that there were 'too many Jews in the towns' and that their numbers should not grow. The drainage of the Oderbruch destroyed the region's biodiversity. The French Jesuit Augustin Barruel in 1797 accused him of a plot with Voltaire, d'Alembert and Diderot against Christianity and kings.
sections.last:
Frederick fought one more, low-scale war, the War of the Bavarian Succession of 1778, to block Joseph II's plan to exchange the Austrian Netherlands for Bavaria. The Prussian and Austrian armies, living off the land and skirmishing in Bohemia, reached a stalemate; Maria Theresa sought peace, Catherine II threatened to join on Frederick's side, and Joseph dropped his claim. When Joseph revived the scheme in 1784, Frederick formed the Fürstenbund, the League of Princes, and won over the Archbishop of Mainz.

In old age he grew solitary as his friends at Sanssouci died, and became more critical and arbitrary, to the frustration of officials and officers. The people of Berlin cheered him and called him Der Alte Fritz, but he preferred the company of his Italian greyhounds. Crippled by asthma and gout in his late 60s and early 70s, he still rose before dawn and drank six to eight cups of coffee a day.

He died in an armchair in his study at Sanssouci on the morning of 17 August 1786, aged 74. He had asked to be buried beside his greyhounds on the vineyard terrace, but his nephew and successor Frederick William II had him entombed beside his father in the Potsdam Garrison Church. Hidden in a salt mine near the end of the Second World War and later moved to Marburg and Burg Hohenzollern, his body was buried in his crypt at Sanssouci on 17 August 1991, as his will had asked.
sections.legacy:
Under Frederick Prussia grew greatly in territory and became a major military power, the fifth and smallest of Europe's great powers. After the Seven Years' War its army was a model copied by Russia and France, and much of the structure of the later German General Staff owed its design to him. Napoleon, at Frederick's tomb in 1807, told his officers, 'Gentlemen, if this man were still alive I would not be here'. Historians such as Robert Citino and Dennis Showalter describe him as the most aggressive and offensive-minded commander of his century.

His memory has been used and disputed. Thomas Carlyle's History of Frederick the Great (1858–1865) made him a hero who shaped history, and nearly all 19th-century German historians turned him into a romantic model of a warrior king. Between 1933 and 1945 the Nazis glorified him as a forerunner of Adolf Hitler, who kept Anton Graff's portrait of him in the Führerbunker. After 1945 his reputation fell in both German states; his equestrian statue was removed from Unter den Linden and put back in 1980, and his standing has grown again in reunified Germany.

Historians in the 21st century tend to see him as an outstanding military leader and capable monarch whose reforms let Prussia contest the Habsburgs for leadership among the German states. The originality of his achievements is debated, as many built on developments already under way, and the label of enlightened absolutist has been questioned because many Enlightenment principles sit poorly with his wars.

summary: Frederick II ruled Prussia from 1740 to 1786. He seized Silesia, kept it through the Seven Years' War at great cost, and annexed most of Royal Prussia in the First Partition of Poland, while reforming the courts and administration and patronising music, letters and science; his reputation has risen and fallen with Germany's own history.

notes: The article gives no casualty totals for the Silesian wars as a whole; only battle figures (Rossbach, Leuthen) and 'almost half his army' at Kunersdorf are used.
His sexuality is given in the article's own hedge ('almost certainly homosexual').
